time_zone: UTC−5 year-round (Quintana Roo) — matches US Eastern in winter, 1h behind in US summer.

english_level: Moderate along the tourist strip; basic Spanish goes a long way inland.
getting_around: Walkable centre, bikes everywhere, cheap taxis and colectivos. No car needed in town.

name: Mexico City
note: Best Sep–Nov & Feb–Apr. Altitude 2,240m. US time zones great for remote work.
description: Mexico's capital sits at 2,240 m in the Valley of Mexico, built over the drained bed of Lake Texcoco. Its 16 boroughs are split into colonias, and most visitors stay in the older districts west of the Zócalo: Roma, Condesa, Juárez and Polanco. A month here is affordable for a city this size: a cappuccino is about MX$68, a basic restaurant meal about MX$200 and a monthly transit pass about MX$360. The Metro, Metrobús and EcoBici bike share cover the central colonias. Público runs coworkings in Roma, Condesa, Juárez and Polanco at roughly MX$3,800–6,500 a month; El 3er Espacio in Condesa charges MX$250 a day. Mexico's median fixed broadband is about 118 Mbps (Ookla). Clocks follow UTC−6 with no daylight saving. Mexico has no dedicated digital nomad visa; remote workers usually apply for temporary residence. The climate is mild thanks to altitude: average highs run from 22°C in December to 27.5°C in April, and nights drop to about 8.5°C in winter. Rain falls mostly from May to October, with July and August the wettest; November to April is dry and sunny. Trade-offs: air pollution and long traffic jams, a city that is sinking from groundwater extraction, earthquake risk, and a central one-bedroom around MX$18,900 a month.

neighbourhoods.name: Roma Norte
neighbourhoods.about: Porfirian mansions, galleries and restaurants around Álvaro Obregón
neighbourhoods.description: Roma was laid out in the early 1900s as an upper-class district just west of the historic centre. Avenida Coahuila divides it into Roma Norte and Roma Sur, and Roma Norte holds most of the colonia's roughly 1,100 listed mansions, many built between 1906 and 1939. Avenida Álvaro Obregón is the main boulevard. Old houses now hold restaurants, bars, cultural centres such as Casa Lamm and galleries along Colima street. Plaza Río de Janeiro, with its fountain and the 1908 Casa de las Brujas, is the old heart of the area. Roma and Condesa together are the centre of the city's café and restaurant scene, which makes Roma Norte the default base for many long-stay visitors. Metro stations sit only at its edges, and the far northeast corner near Metro Cuauhtémoc still has a reputation for crime.
watch_out: Northeast corner near Metro Cuauhtémoc has a reputation for crime
Bars on Álvaro Obregón can be loud at night
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Insurgentes (Metro Line 1) sits on the northwest edge and Chilpancingo (Line 9) on the southern edge; Metrobús and EcoBici cover the interior.

neighbourhoods.name: Condesa
neighbourhoods.about: Art Deco blocks and tree-lined medians around Parque México
neighbourhoods.description: Condesa sits immediately west of Roma and about 4 to 5 km west of the Zócalo. It covers three colonias, Condesa, Hipódromo and Hipódromo Condesa, and many of its apartment buildings date from the 1920s to 1940s, with Art Deco the dominant style. Parque México, built on the site of a former racetrack, is the centre of the area, ringed by the oval of Avenida Ámsterdam with its planted pedestrian median. Parque España is a few blocks away. Most cafés and bars line Ámsterdam and Michoacán. It is one of the greenest and most walkable parts of the city and popular with younger professionals and dog owners. Longtime residents complain about noise from bars, and the Metro only touches the edges of the area.
watch_out: Bar noise on Ámsterdam and Michoacán at weekends
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Chilpancingo and Patriotismo (Metro Line 9) are on the southern edge; Metrobús stops at Sonora, Campeche and Nuevo León on Insurgentes.

neighbourhoods.name: Juárez
neighbourhoods.about: Reforma towers, Zona Rosa and old mansions between Roma and Reforma
neighbourhoods.description: Colonia Juárez is a long triangle between Paseo de la Reforma, Avenida Chapultepec and Avenida Bucareli. It was built from the 1880s for wealthy families leaving the old centre, and many streets are named after European cities, such as Londres, Hamburgo and Berlín. Its best-known part is Zona Rosa, the centre of the city's gay community, with Little Seoul around Hamburgo, Praga, Berna and Biarritz streets. French-style mansions survive on Havre, Berlín and Versalles, and new office and apartment towers rise along Reforma. Juárez is central and well connected, with hotels from budget to the Four Seasons. It is also mixed: parts of Zona Rosa have deteriorated, and residents have complained that poor street lighting has led to crime.
watch_out: Parts of Zona Rosa are run-down and poorly lit at night
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Insurgentes and Cuauhtémoc Metro stations sit on its edges, with Metrobús stops at Hamburgo and Glorieta Insurgentes and EcoBici docks.

neighbourhoods.name: Polanco
neighbourhoods.about: Upscale shopping on Masaryk, embassies and Chapultepec museums
neighbourhoods.description: Polanco is an affluent district in Miguel Hidalgo borough, developed from 1937 on the land of the Hacienda de los Morales. Avenida Presidente Masaryk, its main shopping street, is the most expensive street in Mexico, and the area holds many embassies and top hotels. Part of Chapultepec Park lies within Polanco, including the National Museum of Anthropology and the Museo Tamayo. Parque Lincoln, with its clock tower, is the local park. Restaurants here include Pujol and Quintonil, both awarded two Michelin stars in 2024. It is quieter and more orderly than Roma or Condesa and suits travellers who want security and polish over street life. It is also one of the most expensive property markets in Latin America, and it sits farther from the historic centre.
watch_out: Highest prices in the city for rent, hotels and meals
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Polanco and Auditorio stations on Metro Line 7 serve the area, and the Metrobús Reforma line ends in Polanco.

neighbourhoods.name: Coyoacán
neighbourhoods.about: Colonial plazas, cobbled lanes and Frida Kahlo's Blue House
neighbourhoods.description: Villa Coyoacán, the historic centre of Coyoacán borough, lies about 10 km south of the Zócalo. It is a former independent village of narrow cobblestone streets and small plazas, and the Spanish used it as the first capital of New Spain from 1521 to 1523. Its centre is the pair of plazas Jardín Hidalgo and Jardín del Centenario, with the Parish of San Juan Bautista, a coyote fountain and cafés along the south side. The Frida Kahlo Museum, the Blue House where she was born, is a few blocks north in Colonia del Carmen. On weekdays it is calm and residential, which suits a slower stay. Weekends are different: the borough counts about 70,000 visitors each weekend in the historic centre, and the commute to Roma or the centre is long.
watch_out: Far from Roma, Condesa and the centre
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Viveros/Derechos Humanos and Coyoacán stations on Metro Line 3 are the nearest, though neither is at the plazas; Turibus tours stop in the centre.

neighbourhoods.name: Centro Histórico
neighbourhoods.about: The Zócalo, Templo Mayor and colonial streets of the old city
neighbourhoods.description: The historic centre is built on the ruins of Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital, and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It covers just over 9 km² and 668 blocks, from the Zócalo west to the Alameda Central, with about 1,550 buildings of historical importance. Around the Zócalo stand the National Palace, the Metropolitan Cathedral and the Templo Mayor ruins and museum. Since the early 2000s many streets have been pedestrianised and facades restored, and new restaurants, bars and loft apartments have followed. It is the best base for sightseeing and has the densest Metro coverage in the city. After the shops close, some blocks empty out, and the area still carries a reputation for pickpockets and street vendors crowding the pavements.
watch_out: Some streets empty out and feel unsafe late at night
Pickpockets and street vendors in the busiest streets
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Zócalo/Tenochtitlan and Allende stations on Metro Line 2 serve the core, Bellas Artes the Alameda side, and Metrobús Line 4 crosses the area.

neighbourhoods.name: San Rafael
neighbourhoods.about: Old theatre district with Porfirian houses, now drawing galleries
neighbourhoods.description: San Rafael lies just west of the historic centre, between Ribera de San Cosme and Sullivan street. Founded in the late 19th century, it still has French-style mansions on Sadi Carnot and Rosas Moreno, and 383 of its buildings are catalogued as historic. Known since the 1940s as a theatre district, it still has several stage theatres. The Jardín del Arte has held a Sunday art market on Sullivan street since 1955, and the 1675 San Cosme church stands on the northern edge. Artists and galleries have moved in for its lower rents. It is a working neighbourhood of corner shops, repair workshops and cantinas rather than a tourist district. The trade-offs are traffic cutting through between Insurgentes and the Circuito Interior, street vendors on San Cosme, and street prostitution along Sullivan at night.
watch_out: Sullivan street and Parque Vía are a street-prostitution zone at night
Heavy through traffic and crowded pavements on San Cosme
neighbourhoods.getting_around: San Cosme station on Metro Line 2 opens onto the colonia, and Revolución station is within walking distance; Metrobús stops at Reforma.

best_season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov (dry, mild). Jun–Sep brings daily afternoon rain; Dec–Jan nights get cold.
flight_from_miami: ≈4h direct to MEX, several flights a day.
time_zone: UTC−6 — 1h behind US Eastern in winter, 2h in US summer.
sim_cost: Telcel or AT&T MX ≈ $12–18/mo with 10–20 GB. Coverage excellent.
english_level: Moderate — good in Roma/Condesa/Polanco, patchy elsewhere.
getting_around: Metro and Metrobús are fast and cheap; Uber/DiDi affordable. Traffic is the main tax on your day.
scene: Huge — one of the biggest nomad scenes in the Americas, meetups and coworkings everywhere.

name: Playa del Carmen
best_season: Nov–Apr (dry). May–Oct is hot, humid, with sargassum seaweed on beaches in summer months.
flight_from_miami: ≈2h direct to Cancún (CUN), then 45–60 min shuttle or ADO bus.
time_zone: UTC−5 year-round — matches US Eastern in winter, 1h behind in US summer.
english_level: Widely spoken — the most English-friendly base in Mexico.
getting_around: Very walkable core; colectivos up the coast, ADO buses, cheap taxis.
scene: Large and social — big nomad and expat crowd, coworkings along 5th Avenue and beyond.

name: Mérida
note: Consistently rated the safest major city in Mexico, Mérida combines colonial elegance with proximity to Yucatán's cenotes, Mayan ruins, and Caribbean beaches. sim_cost: Telcel prepaid ≈ $10–15/mo. Coverage good in the city.
